Henri Cartier-Bresson. A French photographer and photojournalist who pioneered the philosophy of the decisive moment—the idea that photography captures a single, unrepeatable instant that crystallises meaning and emotion. His compact Leica camera and street photography style defined twentieth-century photojournalism and influenced generations of photographers worldwide.

Cartier-Bresson developed the concept of the decisive moment, which he called l'instant décisif—the precise split-second when form, gesture, and composition align to create a photograph of maximum emotional and narrative impact. He used the Leica rangefinder camera, a small, fast, unobtrusive tool that allowed him to move through crowds and capture candid moments impossible with the larger press cameras of his era. In 1947 he co-founded Magnum Photos, a cooperative photography agency that established the model for modern photojournalism and allowed photographers to own and control their work.

Cartier-Bresson photographed revolutions, wars, and everyday life across Europe, China, India, and the Americas. His images in publications like Life and Paris Match defined visual journalism for the post-World War II era. He brought a humanist sensibility to documentary photography. His subjects were never exploited or staged, but rather captured in moments of unguarded authenticity.

His work built on the foundation laid by Alfred Stieglitz, the earlier fine-art photographer whose artistic vision and gallery advocacy created the cultural space in which Cartier-Bresson could position photojournalism as art. He shared artistic sensibility with Dorothea Lange, the American documentarian of the Depression era whose social conscience paralleled his humanism, though her idiom was the static portrait. His spontaneous, intuitive approach contrasted sharply with Ansel Adams's rigorous technical mastery.
